subject: Gender Studies
title: VI. Status of Women in Pakistan

segments.text: Women’s health outcomes in Pakistan remain significantly worse than men’s on several key indicators, and understanding why requires looking at both direct healthcare access and the broader social determinants of health.
Key indicators and challenges:

items.text: Maternal mortality.

Pakistan has historically had one of the higher maternal mortality ratios in South Asia, reflecting limited access to skilled birth attendance, particularly in rural areas, alongside early marriage and closely spaced, high-parity pregnancies that increase health risk. While the ratio has declined over recent decades due to expanded health infrastructure and safe motherhood programmes, it remains a significant public health concern, with rural-urban and provincial disparities (Balochistan and rural Sindh generally faring worse than Punjab’s urban centres).
Nutrition.

Cultural food-allocation practices in some households, where men and boys are served first or given priority portions, combined with the additional nutritional demands of frequent pregnancy and breastfeeding, contribute to higher rates of anaemia and malnutrition among women of reproductive age compared to men.
Access barriers.

Women’s healthcare access is shaped by factors beyond clinical availability: the requirement in many households to seek a husband’s or elder’s permission before travelling to a clinic, the shortage of female healthcare providers in conservative rural settings where women may be reluctant to be examined by male doctors (a key rationale behind Pakistan’s Lady Health Worker Programme, launched in 1994 to bring community-based female health workers directly to households), and the financial cost of care in a largely out-of-pocket healthcare financing system.
Reproductive health and family planning.

Access to contraception and family planning services remains limited by cultural attitudes, limited spousal communication about family planning, and uneven rural service availability, contributing to Pakistan’s continued high total fertility rate relative to regional peers.

segments.text: Policy response.

The Lady Health Worker Programme is widely regarded as Pakistan’s most significant structural innovation addressing women’s health access, alongside the Benazir Income Support Programme’s health-linked conditional cash transfers and provincial maternal and newborn health programmes following the 18th Amendment’s devolution of health policy to the provinces.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Maternal mortality, anaemia, and reproductive-health access remain the central challenges, with significant rural-urban and provincial disparities.
Access barriers include not only clinical availability but also permission norms, shortage of female providers, and cost.
The Lady Health Worker Programme (1994) is the key structural policy response bringing care directly to underserved women.

segments.text: Pakistan has made measurable progress in girls’ education over recent decades but continues to show a persistent gender gap, particularly beyond the primary level and in rural areas.
The scale of the gap.

Female literacy in Pakistan remains lower than male literacy nationally, with the gap widening further in rural areas and in provinces such as Balochistan, where girls’ school enrolment and completion rates are markedly lower than boys’. The gap widens progressively at each higher level of education — girls’ enrolment drops relative to boys’ most sharply at the transition from primary to secondary school.
Causes of the gender gap in education:

items.text: Distance and safety.

Because secondary schools are less densely distributed than primary schools, girls in rural areas often must travel further, and safety concerns about travelling alone or with male strangers lead many families to withdraw girls from school at the secondary transition even when they permit primary attendance.
Early marriage.

In some communities, marriage is arranged for girls around or shortly after puberty, directly curtailing further schooling; child marriage remains illegal under Pakistani law (the Child Marriage Restraint Act and later provincial legislation) but continues in practice in some areas due to weak enforcement and social custom.
Household labour demands and opportunity cost.

Families facing economic pressure may prioritise sons’ education, viewed as a future household income investment, over daughters’, particularly where daughters are expected to marry into another household and their education is seen (rightly or wrongly) as benefiting that other family rather than their own.
Shortage of female teachers
, especially in rural secondary schools, discourages families in conservative communities from sending daughters to schools staffed mainly by male teachers.
Direct attacks on girls’ education

in some regions, most visibly the Pakistani Taliban’s campaign against girls’ schooling in Swat (the context for the attack on Malala Yousafzai, covered in Topic 49), represent an extreme but historically significant obstacle in specific areas.

segments.text: Policy responses.

These include stipend and conditional cash transfer programmes specifically incentivising girls’ secondary enrolment (such as province-level girls’ stipend programmes), the recruitment of female teachers for rural schools, and school-security measures following targeted attacks on girls’ education.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Pakistan’s gender gap in education widens at the primary-to-secondary transition and is worse in rural areas and in Balochistan specifically.
Key causes: distance/safety concerns, early marriage, household opportunity-cost calculations, and shortage of female teachers.
Policy responses include girls’ stipend programmes, female teacher recruitment, and school-security measures in areas affected by direct attacks on girls’ education.

segments.text: Pakistan has one of the lowest rates of female labour-force participation in South Asia and among the lowest globally, a fact that international gender-gap indices consistently highlight as a key structural weakness.
Key features of the employment gap:

items.text: Low overall participation.

A large majority of working-age Pakistani women remain outside the formal recorded labour force, though this substantially undercounts women’s actual economic contribution, since much of women’s work — unpaid agricultural labour on family land, unpaid domestic and care work, and informal home-based piecework (such as embroidery or garment stitching) — is not captured in standard labour-force statistics.
Occupational segregation.

Women who are formally employed are concentrated in a narrow range of sectors — education, healthcare/nursing, and certain segments of textiles and garments — with limited representation in higher-paid sectors such as finance, engineering, and senior management.
The gender wage gap.

Even within the same sectors and comparable qualifications, women in Pakistan generally earn less than men, reflecting both direct wage discrimination and the concentration of women in lower-paid roles within each sector.
Legal and workplace barriers.

Despite the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act (2010), enforcement gaps, social stigma around reporting harassment, and limited availability of workplace facilities such as childcare and safe transport continue to constrain women’s willingness and ability to take up or remain in paid work.

segments.text: Structural causes.

These outcomes connect directly to earlier theoretical topics: the sexual division of labour and unpaid domestic burden (Topic 14, Marxist feminism), restrictive social norms around breadwinner masculinity limiting men’s willingness to share domestic responsibilities (Topic 9), and mobility and safety restrictions rooted in prevailing gender norms.
Policy responses and ongoing debate.

These include microfinance and women-targeted vocational training programmes, efforts to expand safe public transport (such as women-only bus services in some cities), and quota-based public-sector employment schemes, though debate continues about whether such targeted interventions can meaningfully shift participation without addressing the underlying unpaid-care burden and mobility restrictions.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Pakistan has among the lowest female labour-force participation rates globally, with substantial undercounting of unpaid and informal work.
Occupational segregation and a persistent gender wage gap characterise formal female employment.
Structural causes trace back to unpaid domestic labour burdens, breadwinner-masculinity norms, and mobility/safety restrictions.

segments.text: Pakistan’s legal framework regarding women’s rights is best understood as a layered and sometimes contested combination of constitutional guarantees, statutory law, and religiously derived law, with a significant history of reform and continuing debate.
Constitutional guarantees.

The Constitution of Pakistan (1973) guarantees equality of citizens before law (Article 25) and explicitly permits the state to make special provisions for the protection of women and children, providing the constitutional basis for affirmative measures such as reserved legislative seats for women (Topic 43).
Key legislative milestones (many already introduced in Topic 23, gathered here with legal specificity):

items.text: The
Hudood Ordinances (1979)
remain historically central because of their controversial treatment of rape and adultery under one combined legal framework, and the
Protection of Women (Criminal Laws Amendment) Act, 2006

, which substantially reformed this by moving rape prosecutions back under the ordinary Pakistan Penal Code framework, requiring a different evidentiary standard than the Hudood zina provisions had required.
The
Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010
, created a formal complaint and inquiry mechanism for workplace sexual harassment across public and private sector organisations.
Provincial
domestic violence legislation

, such as the Punjab Protection of Women against Violence Act (2016) and comparable laws in other provinces, created civil protection orders and support mechanisms for victims of domestic abuse, an area not comprehensively addressed by earlier criminal law.
The
Anti-Honour Killing Laws (Criminal Laws Amendment) Act, 2016

, closed a significant loophole in which victims’ families could “forgive” or reach a compensation settlement (qisas and diyat provisions) with the killer in cases of honour killing, which had previously often allowed perpetrators — sometimes the victim’s own family members who had also brought the case — to escape punishment.
The
Zainab Alert, Response and Recovery Act, 2020
, established a rapid-response mechanism for missing and abducted children following high-profile child sexual abuse and murder cases.

segments.text: Ongoing tensions.

A recurring theme in Pakistani legal debate is the relationship between statutory reform and religiously grounded legal provisions, with reform efforts generally proceeding through arguments grounded in reformist Islamic jurisprudence (ijtihad) to establish that specific reforms are compatible with, rather than opposed to, Islamic legal principles, given the constitutional requirement (under the Objectives Resolution and later constitutional provisions) that laws conform to Islamic injunctions.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Pakistan’s legal framework combines constitutional equality guarantees, ordinary statutory law, and Islamic legal provisions, requiring reform to be argued within an Islamic jurisprudential framework as well as a rights framework.
Key reforms: the 2006 Women’s Protection Act, 2010 Harassment Act, 2016 domestic violence and anti-honour-killing laws, and the 2020 Zainab Alert Act.
The recurring tension is between statutory/constitutional equality provisions and religiously derived legal frameworks, requiring careful, jurisprudentially grounded reform strategies.
